newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy starts again with controversial Priebke case.
newsitem.headline: Italy starts again with controversial Priebke case.

text.p: Former SS captain Erich Priebke goes on trial this week for the second time in a year, accused of complicity in Italy's worst World War Two atrocity, after a previous court decision to free him was overturned.
The 83-year old German will be joined in the dock by ex-Nazi major Karl Hass when the military trial starts on Monday in one of the most controversial cases in recent Italian justice.

Priebke, who is living under house arrest in a Roman Catholic monastery, was found guilty by a military court last year of involvement in the massacre of 335 men and boys in March 1944 in the Ardeatine Caves south of Rome.

But the court, after a three-month trial, said he could not be punished because of extenuating circumstances which triggered a statute of limitation. The verdict, which sparked a storm of protest, was quashed on appeal and a retrial ordered.
The former Nazi said in a newspaper interview published on Sunday he felt he was being victimised.
"There are 22 lawyers against a little captain -- Why?" he told the daily Il Giornale from the San Bonaventura monastery in the wine-producing town of Frascati near Rome.
Priebke, who was extradited from Argentina to Italy in November 1995, admits he shot two victims in the massacre, which included 75 Jews, but says he had to follow orders or be executed himself.
The shootings came as a reprisal for a partisan bomb attack in which 33 troops loyal to the Nazis died.
"For me it was an action of war, I had to obey the order like all the others," Priebke told Il Giornale, adding that he had not thought any more about the killings once the war ended.

Priebke fled to Argentina in 1948 after escaping from a British prisoner of war camp in Italy and said he continued to ask himself why prosecutors had only come to look for him 50 years later. "Why didn't they look for me before?"
The case has a history of controversy and high emotions.

When the first verdict freeing Priebke was handed down last August, protesters besieged the courtroom and stopped Priebke from leaving until Justice Minister Giovanni Maria Flick ordered his re-arrest based on an extradition request by Germany.
The extradition request was turned down in February but in the meantime the original verdict had been thrown out on appeal.
Priebke remained in detention in Rome's Forte Boccea military jail awaiting retrial until he was granted house arrest and moved to Frascati in March on mental health grounds.
In the same month a military court ruled former German SS major Hass, 84, should also stand trial for involvement in the Ardeatine Caves massacre, in which he admits he played a part.
Hass originally returned to Italy as a witness at Priebke's initial trial and is currently under house arrest after fracturing his pelvis trying to flee over a hotel balcony and avoid testifying.
The original verdict, which cited Priebke's age and conduct in Argentina as mitigation, prompted worldwide outrage. Critics branded it a travesty of justice and an insult to the dead.
"August 1, 1996 will go down as a day of infamy in Italian history," said Rabbis Marvin Hier and Abraham Cooper, dean and associate dean of the Los Angeles-based Simon Wiesenthal Centre,
An Israeli Foreign Ministry spokesman called it "a great day for neo-Nazis".
